newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND GIVES GO-AHEAD TO SHIPBUILDING GROUP.
newsitem.headline: POLAND GIVES GO-AHEAD TO SHIPBUILDING GROUP.

text.p: The Polish government gave the go-ahead to a plan to form a holding group of shipyards, their suppliers and banks led by the Stocznia Szczecinska SA, government officials said on Friday.
"A holding group of shipyards, banks and other companies from the shipbuilding sector will be set up by the end of this year," Privatisation Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek told a news conference.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, who also attended the meeting of top government officials, industry heads and bankers in the western port city of Szczecin, said the cabinet had decided to build the group around the Szczecin shipyard.
"We have agreed that the best option is to build an industrial group led by the Szczecin shipyard," Cimoszewicz said.

He said details on the prospective group should be worked out by its would-be members, which should include the Stocznia Gdynia shipyard, the H Cegielski engine maker from the western city of Poznan, the Huta Czestochowa steel mill, several banks and other companies.
Cimoszewicz also pledged government support for the group.

"The government expects from the companies a detailed plan of the holding's development with a timetable....The shipbuilding industry must have a future and the government is offering far-reaching help in its creation," he said.
He said he would offer more details on what would be the government's role in the project within several weeks.
Members of the shipbuilding industry, burdened with debts and hit by a strong zloty, have long signalled that they need to join forces to survive foreign competition.
Last year the industry recorded an aggregate loss of $7 million despite a flood of orders with Szczecin yard, a notable exception, just breaking even on record $460 million sales.
Kaczmarek said the holding's creation should begin with Szczecin and Gdynia shipyards, establishing equity links, and later being grouped with Cegielski.
He said the plan might involve breaking up state-owned Cegielski into two firms, with one producing ship engines entering the holding and the remaining part operating separately.
Kaczmarek also said the plan saw the shipbuilding industry getting a 25-percent share in the holding group. But he said it was too early to discuss details.
Cimoszewicz said the government did not rule out foreign participation in the industrial group but saw no readily available candidates.
"There is no serious foreign offer or a serious foreign investor who could become involved in the holding," he said.
Kaczmarek also said the government agreed to allot 15 percent of Stocznia Szczecinska to its employees for free, boosting their stake to 34 percent and cutting the treasury's stake to six percent.
